messages.subject: Interface for just NUTS / HMC?
parts:
Hi all, I have a problem where I have a target likelihood whose calculation isn't easy to write in a stan model (just trust me), but I can write down approximate gradients which are much easier to compute than the formal gradient calculation and virtually free after the painful likelihood calculation. I'd like to use Stan's implementation of NUTS and HMC adaptation rather than rolling my own (fewer points of failure etc). I don't see it in the documentation, but is there a hook whereby I can pass log-posterior and gradient values and let your implementation of NUTS do the step-size calculations? I see that the LaplacesDemon package has an all-R NUTS that I can probably modify if this isn't doable in Stan.

Thanks,
C Ryan King
University of Chicago

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Interface for just NUTS / HMC?
parts:
I'm afraid there's no way to do this through our R interface.

If you wanted to write it into C++ and add a special distribution
you could use it in Stan. But it's a lot of fussy C++ coding work
that involves understanding our derivatives.




- Bob

On 12/1/13, 11:51 AM, Ryan King wrote:
> Hi all, I have a problem where I have a target likelihood whose calculation isn't easy to write in a stan model (just
> trust me),

We're actually interested in cases like this to guide our
future development, but we understand not everyone is willing
to share model details.
> but I can write down approximate gradients which are much easier to compute than the formal gradient

You have to be careful that the gradients are good enough for
HMC. Bad gradients won't change correctness, but they can seriously
affect speed.

> calculation and virtually free after the painful likelihood calculation. I'd like to use Stan's implementation of NUTS
> and HMC adaptation rather than rolling my own (fewer points of failure etc). I don't see it in the documentation, but is
> there a hook whereby I can pass log-posterior and gradient values and let your implementation of NUTS do the step-size
> calculations?

No. The only way to do that is in our C++ interface, which
requires understanding the way our gradients get calculated
at a much deeper level than the Stan modeling language.

It's something we should think about adding. It could make
some models more efficient than using auto-diff.

Most of the people with hairy log probability functions seem
to use plug-and-play samplers that are gradient free, like
DREAM or emcee.

> I see that the LaplacesDemon package has an all-R NUTS that I can probably modify if this isn't doable in
> Stan.

I'm not trying to spread FUD, but I'd be very careful to
check that you're getting the right answers from another
implementation of NUTS --- there are several subtleties in
the algorithm that affect detailed balance and hence correctness
that we would have messed up had we not had an extensive unit test
suite and developers who understand NUTS and its boundary
conditions.

A good way to test is with simulated data if you can calculate
quantiles and test both those and the posterior means.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Interface for just NUTS / HMC?
parts:
On 12/1/13, 11:51 AM, Ryan King wrote:
> Hi all, I have a problem where I have a target likelihood whose calculation isn't easy to write in a stan model (just
> trust me),

We're actually interested in cases like this to guide our
future development, but we understand not everyone is willing
to share model details.

It's not a secret; it's just complicated and not very general. I have to do a nested simulation step conditional on the current parameters using specialized external code (something like ABC) to compute summary statistics whose distribution I am interested in. On top of that is a method pretty similar to what these people [1] do, where I was hoping to replace gibbs sampling with HMC because of how good it is at generating distant proposals. While it can go in parallel (and those same authors use a specialized ensemble method in another article), I'm cautious about ensemble methods because of the high dimension and how expensive the function evaluations are. Plus, like I mentioned, free derivatives.

[1] projecteuclid.org/euclid.aos/1247836663

Thanks,
C Ryan King
